newsitem.title: MEXICO: Hot money may again drop Mexican peso in hot water.
newsitem.headline: Hot money may again drop Mexican peso in hot water.

text.p: The flightiness of foreign capital and the shifting economic fortunes of rival nations may be leaving Mexico's temperamental peso open to trouble, economists say.

So far this year, the peso has wrong-footed most market analysts who have been surprised by its persistent strength and by the record-breaking surge in Mexican stocks that has helped bolster the currency.
Still, some economists are warning against complacency, arguing the inflows of short-term foreign investments in stock and other liquid assets have traditionally been Mexico's Achilles' heel.
"The potential volatility of foreign capital still represents one of Mexico's main vulnerable points," said Javier Murcio, director of emerging markets for Latin America at CSFB.

"The risk is that any potentially sudden shift in sentiment towards the Mexican bolsa, or a shift in flows back to Asia in pursuit of perceived cheaper opportunities under a stabilized situation, could bring a rapid adjustment in the peso," he said.
Bankers Trust economist Denis Parisien agreed the composition of current capital flows may pose a risk.

"There is a fairly significant proportion that is not hot money, but in absolute terms there is definitely more hot money that has flowed into the system, in the year-to-date, than last year," he said.
"Portfolio flows are up -- there is definitely that exposure to outflows," he added.
Foreign investment in Mexican securities climbed 15.64 percent in July alone, and the bolsa has powered to a series of record highs over the past month.
During the same month, the currency strengthened by 10 centavos, or 1.3 percent, against the dollar, and some economists estimate it is now about 10 percent overvalued.
The longer the peso goes unadjusted, they say, the harder the fall -- bringing echoes of the 1994 crash.

Mexico plunged into an economic crisis in December 1994 when its overvalued currency, a hefty current account deficit and U.S. interest rate rises were mixed in a dangerous cocktail with an overdependence on short-term foreign capital flows.

To be sure, the current economic fundamentals are stronger than they were in 1994 and the current account in better shape. Still, the volume of cash flowing into the country and its impact on foreign exchange rates is worrying some economists.

They will not have a clear picture of exactly how much hot money is flowing into the country until the Bank of Mexico publishes second-quarter current account numbers -- due within 90 days of the quarter's end.

But the strong flows registered so far mean the peso -- which many had forecast would depreciate around the July 6 Mexican elections -- may end the year far stronger than analysts had originally expected.

A central bank survey of 28 economists, obtained by Reuters at the start of August, showed an average downward revision of 17 centavos from month-earlier forecasts to a year-end level of 8.39 to the dollar.
Last week CSFB adjusted its year-end outlook to 8.2 pesos per dollar, while Bankers Trust said it was looking for 8.09.
On Thursday the currency closed at 7.76 to the dollar, at the stronger end of this year's surprisingly narrow trading range of 7.78 to 8.03.

Mexico's 1994-95 financial crisis is now being mirrored in Thailand, whose defacto devaluation last month plunged the country's economy into turmoil and required an International Monetary Fund bailout.

While Mexican markets have benefited from capital flight out of Thailand and its shaken Asian neighbors, economists say such flows are just as likely to reverse direction and constitute the weak link in Mexico's economic chain.
"At the first sign of danger, at least some market participants are very willing to get out of pesos," one analyst said. "The true market impact of those participants is, as of yet, still unknown."
